chapter_theme: Poems 61 to 80 praise Chola and Pandya kings and test what kingship is worth: the double death of two kings in one battle, the honour death after Venni and a poet ranking the loser over the victor, guide poems sending hungry bards to Chola patrons, three royal vows that stake justice, friendship, fame and giving, a captive king's refusal to beg, a king on the lightness of the throne, and the boy-king Neduncheliyan's single victory over seven.

61.reading: The poet paints the plenty of Chenni's farmland, where weeding women eat fresh rice with thick slices of fish and the labourers' children, tired of coconuts, climb the straw stacks to reach for palmyra fruit, and then says that whoever challenges this king learns his fate: no one who fought him has been seen to live, and no one who bowed at his feet has been seen to suffer.
61.nuance: The last lines set two fates side by side: those who fight him do not live, and those who come to fit themselves to his feet (திருந்து அடி பொருந்த) do not suffer. The praise of might is also an offer of protection, and the farm scene of children too full to want coconuts is what that protection yields.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed praised is the king's sure victory over all who fight him

comparisons.tenor: the king's firm shoulders

62.reading: Asking what victory there can be in such a war, the poet describes a field where both kings, who fought by the rule of right, have died together with their armies: demon women dance with bloodied hands to the drum, the umbrellas shake, the drums are silent, no one is left to claim the field, the queens refuse the widow's greens and cold bath and lie down on their husbands' breasts, and only the gods in their unfading world gain guests; the poet ends 'may your fame flourish'.
62.nuance: The opening question (அமர்மிகல் யாவது?) and the closing blessing frame the poem as counsel against such war: the only party that gains is heaven, which gets its guests. The queens who neither eat the widow's greens nor take the cold bath but settle on their husbands' breasts are, on the plain sense, dying with them; the poem states it without comment.

thinai_evidence.note: a battle in which both sides fell, which is the thumbai situation of the whole field destroyed

63.reading: After a battle in which the elephants, horses, warriors and drums are all lost and both kings have fallen on the field, the poet asks what will now become of their wide, rich lands, where women with bangles of lily stalk eat fresh flattened rice and dive into cool water.
63.nuance: Each line of the catalogue ends on a verb of ending (ஒழிந்தனவே, பட்டனவே, மாய்ந்தனரே, விளிந்தனவே), and the drums die 'for want of anyone to carry them'. The question at the end turns from the dead to the living land, which now has no king; the poem counts the cost to the country rather than the glory.

thinai_evidence.note: both kings died in the fight, the thumbai matter of mutual destruction

64.reading: The speaker urges a dancing woman with few bangles to pack her lute and small drums and set out with him to see Kudumi, the king of great honour who stays on in the enemy's land on the battlefield where elephant herds fought and vultures wheel over the fresh flesh, so that they may leave behind their thin watery gruel.
64.nuance: The gift is never named; it is implied by what the travellers will leave behind, their watery gruel. The king is to be found not in his capital but in the enemy's country, so the dancer is sent to a war camp.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer directs a dancer to a king's gift, the guide-poem form of praise

65.reading: The drums and lutes are forgotten, the great pots are overturned and the butter gone, kin forget the toddy, the ploughmen's call and the village festivals are forgotten, because, as at the full moon when sun and moon face each other and one sinks behind the hill in the sad evening, the warrior king, ashamed of a wound in his back from a king his equal, has sat facing north with his sword to die; here the days no longer pass as days.
65.nuance: The full-moon image fits the event closely: two lights of equal rank face each other and one goes down, as two equal kings met and one withdrew. The shame named is of the wound's place (புறப்புண், a wound on the back), not of losing, and the five 'forgets' (மறப்ப) show a whole country stopping its music, food and work.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament over a king's chosen death, which the Tholkappiyam places with the passing of the world (kaanchi), though the colophon files it under pothuviyal

comparisons.tenor: the king withdrawing to die while his equal remains

66.reading: Addressing Karikal Valavan, descendant of the one who drove ships over the sea by mastering the wind, the poet grants that he went and won and showed his strength, then asks whether the king who, ashamed of a wound on his back at the field of Venni, sat facing north and reached the world of great fame is not a better man than he.
66.nuance: The praise is real for four lines and then turns: the victor is told to his face that the defeated king, by his death, is the better man. The poem does not name him; the colophon of 65 and the line புறப்புண் நாணி, shared with 65, identify him as Cheralathan.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem weighs excellence in war, the matter of vaakai, and gives the palm to the loser

67.reading: In an evening when the moon with joined horns shines like the bright face of the victorious lord who guards the land and the poet is helpless with longing, he asks a swan, if it flies north after eating fish at the ford of Kumari and passes through the Chola country, to alight on the high mansion at Kozhi, enter the palace without waiting at the gate, and say within the hearing of the great king Killi that it serves at the feet of Pisir Aandhai; then the king will give it his own beloved jewels for its mate to wear.
67.nuance: The bird messenger and the helpless evening are akam devices, here turned to a poet's longing for a king. The only credential the swan is to carry is the poet's name, and the poet is sure it will open the palace without a wait at the gate; the poem shows the bond by what it expects the name to do.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's regard for the poet, which is iyanmozhi praise

comparisons.tenor: the evening moon

68.reading: The poet asks a bard, whose kin have ribs that stand out like a skinned monitor lizard's and who is weary of patrons who barely listen, why he lingers here, and tells him of the lord at Uranthai, gentle to women and binding men by strength, whose Kaveri nourishes the people like a mother's milk to a newborn, where warriors with no war to go to beat their shoulders and the drum sounds, and elephants wallow in mud of spilled toddy; if the bard goes, the lord will give so much that he forgets other men's doors.
68.nuance: Lines 11 and 12 are hard: the warriors seem to complain that, inner enmity having been settled, the king will not send them against foes, so they will die idle; the sense of புட்பகை is not certain. Either way the warriors' frustration is praise of a peaceful land. பிறன்கடை மறப்ப names the bard's real wish: an end to going from door to door.

thinai_evidence.note: a poet directs a hungry bard to a patron, the guide-poem form of praise

comparisons.tenor: the bard's family, their ribs showing from hunger
the Kaveri feeding the people

69.reading: To a bard with a lute in hand, hunger in his body for want of patrons and a patched rag at his waist, whose large family is wan like the body of a man with no resolve, the poet says: go to Killi Valavan of Uranthai of tall mansions, whose army made the battle camp a field of flesh; you will not even wait at his gate, and once you have seen him in his court where he gives away chariots, you will not fail to wear a golden lotus that no bee hums over.
69.nuance: The opening inventory (கையது, மெய்யது, அரையது: in the hand, in the body, at the waist) makes the bard's poverty a list of possessions, the last of them hunger. The lotus that no bee visits is a gold lotus, the bard's ornament from the king.

thinai_evidence.note: a poet directs a hungry bard to a patron, the guide-poem form of praise

comparisons.tenor: the bard's starving family
the king's gold ornament

70.reading: The poet tells a bard who keeps asking whether his drum will at last be heard with pleasure and his hunger eased that if he goes slowly with his dancer, past the village of Pannan the open-handed where bees hum over the white lily, to Killi Valavan, whose city's food never runs low however much is taken, like a cool pond in the month of Thai, and which knows only the cooking fire and never the fire that burns towns, he will arrive; his giving is no windfall like woodcutters stumbling on gold, so the bard need not doubt it.
70.nuance: அடுதீ அல்லது சுடுதீ அறியாது, only the fire that cooks and never the fire that burns, makes the king's land a land without war. The last comparison is a negated one: the gift is not like a lucky find, because a lucky find cannot be counted on; the poem praises the giver's reliability, not only his wealth. Pannan, another patron, is named in passing on the road.

thinai_evidence.note: a poet directs a bard to a patron, the guide-poem form of praise

comparisons.tenor: the kinai drum, its frame braced with fine rods
the city's store of food that never lessens
the king's giving, said to be unlike a windfall

71.reading: Boothappandiyan vows that if he does not strike the kings who, raging like lions, say they have joined to fight him, and see their backs as they flee with their chariots, he may be parted from his wife of wide painted eyes, may become a king who in his assembly put an incapable man in office out of fondness and wielded a weak sceptre against right, and may lose the joy of his friends, the lord of Maiyal, Maavan, Aanthai, Anthuvan Saathan, Aathan Azhisi, Iyakkan and the rest, and be born to guard others' harsh lands instead of the southern land of his line.
71.nuance: The curses form a ranked set of the three things a king holds dear: his wife, his justice and his friends, and then his birthright. The friends are named one by one; the poem keeps a roll of a Pandya court's companions. The lion comparison uses the comparative case ending (மடங்கலின், 'than / like a lion') rather than அன்ன or போல.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's vow that stakes everything he holds, which the colophons place under kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the enemy kings' rage
the king's friends

72.reading: Neduncheliyan vows that if he does not shatter and capture with their drums the angry kings who mocked him as a boy and, trusting their elephants, chariots, horses and warriors, spoke small words, then may his people, finding no cool shade under his umbrella, weep and blame him as a cruel king; may the poets led by Maangudi Maruthan cease to sing of his land; and may he know the poverty of having nothing to give suppliants while those he keeps suffer.
72.nuance: What the king stakes is telling: not death or defeat but his people's tears and blame, the silence of poets, and the inability to give. A king's worst fate is to be a cruel sceptre, unsung and ungiving. The mockery 'he is young' (இளையன் இவன்) recurs as the enemies' boast in 78.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's vow that stakes his justice, fame and giving, which the colophons place under kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the protection of the king's rule

73.reading: Nalankilli says that if men come gently, touch his feet and ask, the kingdom he inherited with its drums is a small thing to give and he would give even his life; but the fool who ignored the strength of the strong and scorned him will hardly escape alive, like a blind man who has stumbled on a sleeping tiger; and if he does not crush them like a hard bamboo shoot caught under the foot of a cane-eating elephant, may his garland wither in the reluctant embrace of women who feel no love.
73.nuance: The vow sets giving and fighting as two answers to the same kingdom: asked humbly, the king gives it away, even with his life; taken by scorn, he defends it. The curse he accepts is the embrace of women who do not love him, a shame of pleasure rather than of war.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's vow, which the colophons place under kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the fool who scorned the king

comparisons.vehicle: கழைதின் யானைக் கால் அகப் பட்ட வன்றிணி நீண்முளை
comparisons.tenor: the enemies the king will crush

74.reading: The poet-king asks whether a warrior line that will not let even a child who dies, or a lump of flesh born dead, go without the sword's cut, saying it did not die a man's death, would ever bear a son like him, who, held in trouble like a chained dog, without strength, begs to quench the fire in his belly a little water given in charity by men who are no kin.
74.nuance: The poem leaves its subject implicit and puts it as a question: the speaker is the one who begs, and the question says such a lineage could not have borne him. The colophon here gives no circumstance; the chain and the begging for a drink are in the poem, but who holds him is not said. The sword-cut given to the dead child shows a code in which even death must be a warrior's.

thinai_evidence.note: a statement of the shame of a life kept by begging, a kaanchi matter of honour above life, though the colophon files it under pothuviyal

comparisons.tenor: the speaker held in bonds

75.reading: When the elders have gone to death and the ancient heritage of rule comes by right, a petty man of blunt manhood who thinks 'we have gained greatness' and begs dues from his people will think it a great thing, but if a worthy man whose strong legs bear the brunt of battle gets it, the fortune of kings with drums and sky-high white umbrella is as light as the dry stick of the white kidai plant withered by summer beside a dried-up pond.
75.nuance: The petty heir's mark is that he 'begs' from his own people (குடிபுரவு இரக்கும்): taxing is named as asking. The worthy man's lightness about the throne is not renunciation; it comes from his strength in war, the நோன்தாள் that bears battle.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem defines the excellent king against the petty one, a vaakai matter of excelling in one's part, though the colophon files it under pothuviyal

comparisons.tenor: the royal fortune in the eyes of the worthy heir

76.reading: Killing one another and being killed is nothing new; it is the way of this world; but never till today had we heard of this: seven kings with ornate anklets, not knowing the might and greatness of Cheliyan, who wears a honey-dripping garland of neem shoots twined with uzhinai and goes to the sound of the clear kinai drum, came together saying 'we will fight', and he alone fought and destroyed their strength on the field.
76.nuance: The opening concedes that killing is commonplace so that the novelty of one against seven stands out: the wonder the poem names is of the new (இன்றின் ஊங்கோ கேளலம்). The neem is the Pandya's emblem and the uzhinai the flower of siege.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's single victory over seven is the excellence in war that vaakai praises

77.reading: Who is this who stands gracing the front of his tall chariot, the warrior's anklet on legs that have only just shed a child's tinkling anklets, neem shoots and uzhinai on a brow just shorn of its tuft, a bow in a hand just stripped of small bangles? Long live his garland! He has put on the garland but not yet taken off the child's amulet; weaned from milk, he ate rice only today; he neither marvelled at nor looked down on the fresh warriors who came at him from every side, and when he seized them and killed them so they fell to the ground he neither rejoiced nor scorned them.
77.nuance: Each line pairs a child's thing just removed with a warrior's thing just put on, so the boy's age is told entirely through objects. The praise ends on his evenness of mind: no wonder at the enemy, no contempt, no gloating after the kill.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises a young king's excellence in battle

78.reading: The new warriors who came scorning my lord, whose broad chest rises to battle like a tiger leaving its den for prey, saying 'we are great and many, the fighter is young and the plunder large', went back with dull eyes and turned their backs; not content to kill them here, he followed them to their fathers' town and, to the sound of the clear drum, killed them there, so that their jewelled women passed away in shame.
78.nuance: The enemies' boast (பொருநனும் இளையன், 'the fighter is young too') answers to the taunt in 72; here it is reported from the other side and punished. Pursuing them to their fathers' town makes the defeat a shame for their families, not only for themselves.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's victory over those who scorned his youth

comparisons.tenor: the king's chest rising to battle

79.reading: Having bathed in the cool pond at the gate of the old town and put on bright neem leaves from the common tree, walking like an elephant before the clear kinai drum, Cheliyan of the fierce war has come; the new warriors facing him are many; will any of them be left, when the day is far too short?
79.nuance: The question at the end is a boast put as worry: the day is too short for him to kill so many, not too short for them to beat him. The ritual bath and the neem from the common tree (மன்ற வேம்பு) show the king's going to war as a public rite.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's certain victory

comparisons.tenor: Cheliyan's gait as he goes to battle

80.reading: At Amur of sweet strong toddy the wrestler crushed the might of a mighty wrestler, pressing one leg on his chest and with the other bracing against his rush; let Tittan, whether he looks kindly on him or not, see how the wrestler who enters the field conquers and kills, bending his foe at both ends like a hungry elephant trying to break a bamboo.
80.nuance: The poem wants a particular witness: Tittan, 'whether he grants or not' (நல்கினும் நல்கான் ஆயினும்), so the hero's standing with Tittan is in question and the fight is offered as proof. The poem does not say what Tittan is to the hero; the colophon names the hero as Perunarkilli.

thinai_evidence.note: single combat to the death is a thumbai matter

comparisons.tenor: the wrestler bending his opponent

links.note: Akananuru 55's mother, sleepless after her daughter's elopement, compares her lot to the noble men who, hearing Cheralathan's bitter words when he sat north after Venni, went with him to the other world; 65 laments the same king's sitting north (வடக்கு இருந்தனன்) out of shame at a back wound.
links.teaches: The akam poet can use the king's death as a simile for a mother's loss only because puram poems such as 65 had made it known, and the akam poem adds what 65 does not say: that men of his court followed him into death, so the two together give the event and its aftermath.

links.note: Both poems are on the death after Venni: 65 mourns the king who sat north ashamed of a back wound, and 66, addressed to the victor Karikal, says that king is better than him; both use the phrase புறப்புண் நாணி.
links.teaches: Read together they show the honour code reversing a battle's result: the loser's chosen death, mourned in 65 as the stopping of a whole country's life, is used in 66 to rank him above the victor, said to the victor's face.

links.note: Akananuru 246's friend says the gossip about the hero was louder than the uproar at Venni when Karikal broke the strength of kings and eleven Velir and their drums were left on the field.
links.teaches: The akam poet remembers Venni for the noise of Karikal's victory over many kings, while 66 remembers it for the defeated king's honourable death, so one battle served akam as a measure of loudness and puram as a lesson in honour.

links.note: Kural 970 says the world praises the radiance of those who will not live when disgrace comes; 66 says the king who sat north ashamed of his wound reached the world of great fame (மிகப் புகழ் உலகம்).
links.teaches: 66 shows what the Kural's general praise of honour could mean in practice: a dishonour as small as a wound's place on the body, a death chosen for it, and a poet ranking the dead man above the living victor in public.

links.note: The half-line எழுவர் நல்வலம் அடங்க (the strength of the seven brought down) stands in 76 line 12 and in Akananuru 36 line 20, both of Cheliyan's victory at Alankanam; Akananuru 36 names the seven kings.
links.teaches: The identical half-line shows that the Alankanam victory had a fixed formula that passed from praise poetry into akam, where the war-cry of that day becomes the measure of how loud the town's gossip is about the hero's new bride.

links.note: 76 opens: killing and being killed is not new (புதுவது அன்று), it is the way of the world; 192 says dying is not new (சாதலும் புதுவது அன்றே).
links.teaches: The same commonplace serves opposite ends: in 192 the oldness of death leads to calm toward great and small alike, while in 76 it is granted only so that one king's feat can stand out as the thing never heard of before.

links.note: In 72 the king accepts, if he breaks his vow, that his people will find no shade under his rule and will weep and blame him as cruel; Kural 555 says the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering are what wear away a king's wealth.
links.teaches: The Kural names the people's tears as a force that destroys a king's wealth; 72 shows a king himself choosing those tears as the worst penalty he could stake, so the Kural's warning was already a ruler's own measure of failure.

links.note: In 72 the kings mock Neduncheliyan as a boy (இளையன் இவன்); in 78 the new warriors say 'the fighter is young' (பொருநனும் இளையன்) and are pursued to their fathers' town and killed.
links.teaches: 78 tells, through a court poet, the sequel that 72 vows in the king's own voice, so the anthology keeps both the vow and its fulfilment, and the taunt of youth becomes the hinge of the king's fame.

links.note: 77 pictures the king as a boy just weaned, with the child's amulet still on; 72 is the same king's vow against kings who mocked him as young.
links.teaches: 77 shows that the enemies' taunt in 72 was literally true, which makes the boy's vow and its performance the more striking and explains why his poets kept returning to his age.

links.note: Among the curses 71 accepts is to put an incapable man in office in his assembly out of fondness (அன்பின் அவையத்துத் திறன்இல் ஒருவனை நாட்டி); Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every kind of folly.
links.teaches: The Kural names fondness as the cause of a bad appointment; 71 shows how grave such an appointment was held to be, since a king lists it among the curses on himself beside losing his wife, his friends and his birthright.

links.note: 73 says the fool who ignored the strength of the strong (ஆற்றல் உடையோர் ஆற்றல் போற்றாது) will hardly escape alive; Kural 891 says not slighting the strength of those able to act (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் இகழாமை) is the chief of all safeguards.
links.teaches: The near-identical wording shows the Kural turning a king's threat into a general safeguard: what 73 says from the side of the strong man about to strike, the Kural says to everyone who might provoke him.

links.note: 74 asks whether a warrior line would bear a son who begs a little drink to quench his hunger; Kural 1066 says even asking water for a cow degrades the tongue more than anything.
links.teaches: The Kural makes asking shameful even for the worthiest cause; 74 roots the same horror in a warrior code that will not let even a stillborn child go unmarked by the sword, so the shame of begging is shown as a matter of lineage as well as of general ethics.

links.note: 75's petty heir begs dues from his people (குடிபுரவு இரக்கும்); Kural 552 says the asking (இரவு) of a king with his sceptre is like a robber with a spear saying 'hand it over'.
links.teaches: Both books call a king's demand on his people begging, and 75 adds the cause the Kural leaves out: the petty heir values the throne as wealth to take from, where the worthy one counts the same fortune as light as a dry stick.

links.note: In 67 Pisir Aandhai trusts that King Killi will reward a swan for saying it serves at his feet; in 216 Kopperuncholan tells his doubting courtiers that the poet, whom he knows only by hearing, will come.
links.teaches: Each partner stakes something on the other's regard for a name alone: the poet promises the king's gift for it, the king promises the poet's arrival, so the anthology keeps this friendship from both sides.

links.note: 68 promises the bard a lord who will give so much that he forgets other men's doors (பிறன்கடை மறப்ப); Kural 1053 says even asking has a grace when one stands before those who hide nothing and know their duty.
links.teaches: The Kural allows asking only before the right giver, and the guide poem is the bard's practical answer: it tells him which door to stand at so that he need never stand at another, which shows ஆற்றுப்படை solving the Kural's problem of asking.

links.note: 70 says the king's giving is no windfall like woodcutters finding gold; Kural 216 likens the wealth of the good-hearted man to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town.
links.teaches: 70 makes explicit what the Kural's tree in the town only implies: the value of a generous man's wealth to those who ask is that it can be counted on, unlike a lucky find, so reliability is part of what giving means.

links.note: Both poems, by Kazhathalaiyar and Paranar, are on the battle in which Neduncheralathan and Peruvirarkilli both died; both list the fallen army and silent drums and both kings dead.
links.teaches: Two poets on the same double death close differently, one with heaven's feast and a blessing on fame, the other with a question about the orphaned land, so the thokai nilai could console with glory or count the cost to the country.

links.note: Akananuru 6 calls Tittan of Uranthai the great giver who brings the wealth of rain (மாவண் தித்தன்); 80 asks Tittan to witness the hero's victory 'whether he grants or not' (நல்கினும் நல்கான் ஆயினும்).
links.teaches: The akam poet uses Tittan's fame as a giver as a byword, while 80 makes his grace toward one man uncertain, so the same chief appears as a public giver and as a withholding judge whose favour must be won.

new_concepts.gloss: a warrior's or king's vow, made before battle, that names the penalties he accepts if he fails
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons of 71, 72 and 73 (வஞ்சினக் காஞ்சி); the poems themselves do not use the word

new_concepts.gloss: sitting facing north to fast unto death, a chosen death for honour
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use it: வடக்கு இருந்தனன் in 65 line 11, வடக் கிருந்தோனே in 66 line 8

new_concepts.gloss: a guide poem: a performer directs another performer to a patron's gift

source_issues: 72 line 1 reads நகுதத் கனரே; the word is very likely நகுதக் கனரே (a doubled த for க). Left as it stands.
69 line 7: the text flag records முழுவதுடன் against முழுதுடன் in the two editions; the metre favours முழுதுடன். Our reading kept.

77 line 13: the text flag records இகழ்ந்தன்றும் against மலிந்தன்றும் (TVU) and மலிந்தன்று (Duraisamy Pillai). Marked as it stands; the sense 'neither rejoiced nor gloated' is close either way. Line 1 also reads ஓண் கழல், probably for ஒண் கழல்.
77: the review's line table gives our text 10 lines against the site's 13, but our current text has 13 lines; the table looks out of date for this poem.

64, 72, 74: the review notes the site lacks our opening line; in all three our line 1 is needed for the sense (the packing of the instruments in 64, the mockery in 72, the dead child in 74), so the loss is the site's.
65: the colophon patron field holds a sentence on the circumstance (that he fought Karikal, was wounded in the back and sat north), not only a name.
